summary: Proposes two extensions to the Domain Name System. One is a method for storing and looking up records that map between network names and numbers, which is a proposed standard. The other is a set of ideas for describing mappings between arbitrary identifiers and numbers.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1101 describes how DNS can store network names alongside network numbers. It also proposes an experimental pattern for mapping other identifiers to numbers.

questions: how to map network names to numbers in dns
how to find network name from ip address
how does dns store a network name
subtitle: A DNS method for mapping network names to numbers and an experimental mapping framework.

tldr.problem: DNS can map host names to addresses, but the RFC identifies a need to map network names to network numbers as well.
tldr.mechanism: It stores network-name pointers at host-zero names in IN-ADDR.ARPA, uses address records for subnet masks and proposes a general DNS tree pattern for other name-to-number mappings.
tldr.outcome: The RFC calls its network-name method a proposed standard and its general Yellow Pages mapping ideas experimental. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

today: The unit metadata records RFC 1101's status as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its own status section calls the network-name method a proposed standard and the general mapping ideas experimental.

sections.title: Why DNS Network Names Are Useful
sections.content:
The RFC notes that DNS maps host names to IP addresses but did not provide the network-name mapping available in HOSTS.TXT. Such names can help debugging tools and status displays.

The document proposes a specific network-name arrangement and separately discusses a general pattern for mappings such as TCP-port names to numbers. The two proposals have different status in the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS already maps host names to addresses. This RFC adds a way to look up the name of a network from its number.

sections.title: Storing Network Names
sections.content:
The network-name method uses host-zero addresses in the IN-ADDR.ARPA tree. A PTR record at that name points to the network name. An A record can also give an address mask when the network contains subnets.

The network name itself can point back to the host-zero entry, and an organization's name can point to the networks it has. These records allow lookups from network number to name and from name to network number.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS stores links between a network name and a special address name under IN-ADDR.ARPA. A subnet mask can identify another level of subnet information.

sections.title: Looking Up a Network and Its Subnets
sections.content:
To look up a network from an IP address, the procedure masks the address to the network boundary, reverses the octets and queries the corresponding PTR name under IN-ADDR.ARPA. The RFC gives 10.0.0.51 as an example, which produces the query name 0.0.0.10.IN-ADDR.ARPA.

To find nested subnets, the resolver checks for an A record containing a mask and repeats the lookup using that mask. It stops when the next entry has no mask record.
sections.plainLanguage: A lookup converts the address to the network number and forms a reversed IN-ADDR.ARPA name. A mask can direct the next lookup to a subnet.

sections.title: The Experimental Yellow Pages Pattern
sections.content:
The RFC calls a precomputed DNS index for mapping one kind of identifier to another a Yellow Pages (YP). It proposes names that identify the input type, output type and YP origin, so a lookup has a known place in the DNS tree.

Examples discussed include TCP port names and numbers, protocol identifiers, autonomous-system identifiers and network names. The RFC presents these structures as ideas for future mappings, not as a single required global index.
sections.plainLanguage: The general pattern organizes a lookup by the kind of value being searched and returned. The RFC presents it as an experimental approach for other mappings.
